articles.title: RFL CEO ian Nolan visits Rochdale Hornets at crown oil arena
articles.excerpt: Ian Nolan's visit to Rochdale Hornets marks a significant moment for the club and the local rugby league community.
articles.content_html:
During his visit, Nolan engaged with the Hornets' operation, discussing both sporting and community perspectives. His presence was welcomed by the club, with officials expressing optimism about the future of rugby league outside the Super League.

Andy Mazey, a representative of Rochdale Hornets, expressed his honour in welcoming Nolan, highlighting the positive impact of his arrival on the club and the wider rugby league community.

Nolan is recognized for his enthusiasm and innovative approach to the sport, which has brought a sense of optimism to the Hornets.

articles.title: Rochdale Hornets confirm opponents for 2027 1895 Cup group phase
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Hornets will face six teams in the opening phase of the 2027 1895 Cup, including Dewsbury Rams and Newcastle Thunder.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Hornets have confirmed their opponents for the opening phase of the 2027 1895 Cup, which includes six fixtures against teams such as Dewsbury Rams and Newcastle Thunder.

The Hornets will play three home matches and three away matches against Goole Vikings (away), Dewsbury Rams (home), Keighley Cougars (home), Doncaster (away), Hunslet (away), and Newcastle Thunder (home).

The competition will adopt a Champions League-style format, with results contributing to a single table for all participating teams.

The exact dates for these fixtures will be announced when the full fixture list is released on Sunday.

This format aims to enhance the competitive nature of the tournament, culminating in an open draw for the quarter-finals and a final scheduled for the August Bank Holiday weekend.

The 1895 Cup is a significant event in the rugby league calendar, providing clubs with the opportunity to showcase their talent and compete for silverware. Fans can look forward to an exciting season ahead as the Hornets prepare for their matches.

articles.title: Castleton headteacher Lindsay Torrance wins lifetime achievement award
articles.excerpt: Lindsay Torrance, retired headteacher of Castleton Primary, received a lifetime achievement award at the Raising Rochdale Education Awards after 43 years in education.
articles.content_html:
Lindsay Torrance, retired headteacher of Castleton Primary School, has been awarded a lifetime achievement accolade at the Raising Rochdale Education Awards, recognising her 43 years of dedication to education.

Torrance, who served as headteacher at Castleton Primary since 1998, retired in July 2026 after 28 years in that role.

Her commitment to teaching and her strong connection to the Rochdale community were highlighted by her colleagues and local parents, who nominated her for the award.

At the ceremony, which celebrated various achievements in local education, Torrance expressed her joy in teaching, stating that working with children has been a fulfilling experience.

Seventeen other awards were presented during the event, with Falinge Park High School receiving the Leadership Team of the Year award.

articles.title: You may be able to claim for Turner Brothers asbestos
articles.excerpt: Former workers, their families and people who lived near the Spotland factory can still claim, and there are routes for people exposed elsewhere too.
articles.content_html:
People made ill by asbestos from the former Turner Brothers Asbestos factory in Spotland can still claim compensation, 25 years after the company collapsed.

Former workers can claim, and so can people who never worked there, such as relatives exposed to dust on work clothes and people who lived near the factory.

Claims linked to Turner Brothers are handled by the T&N UK Asbestos Trust, which holds a separate fund for Turner Brothers claims. Its website is tandnasbestos.org.uk.

The trust usually pays a set share of a claim's full value rather than the whole amount.

People exposed to asbestos at other workplaces may also be able to claim, even if their employer closed long ago. Mesothelioma, a cancer caused by asbestos, often takes 40 to 50 years to show symptoms.

An employer's insurer is usually responsible even when the firm no longer exists. The Employers' Liability Tracing Office, at elto.org.uk, helps people find a former employer's insurer, though it does not pay compensation itself.

People diagnosed with mesothelioma who cannot trace a liable employer or insurer may be able to claim from the government's Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme, which pays according to age.

A government lump sum under the Pneumoconiosis etc. (Workers' Compensation) Act 1979 covers certain dust-related diseases when damages cannot be won from an employer, often because it has stopped trading. The claim form helpline is 0800 279 2322.

A separate 2008 mesothelioma scheme covers people exposed through a relative's work clothes, and people who cannot say where they were exposed but were exposed only in the UK.

Since 31 October 2026, dependants claiming under either government scheme after a sufferer died without claiming receive the full amount the sufferer would have been paid.

For a 60-year-old claimant under the 2008 scheme, that raises a dependant's payment from £24,526 to £56,656, according to the government. The change applies to new claims only.

Asbestos products were made at the Spodden Valley site from 1879 until 1998, and it was once the world's largest asbestos textile factory. Turner & Newall went into administration in 2001.

The site's owner, Spodden Park Ltd, began investigation works this month to map where asbestos is buried, ahead of a clean-up and redevelopment.

Compensation claims generally have to begin within three years of diagnosis, or within three years of a death. Some government payments must be claimed within 12 months.

The Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group, a registered charity, gives free advice on benefits and compensation to people with any asbestos-related disease, and runs support groups for patients and bereaved families.

The group can be contacted on 0161 258 0166, Monday to Friday from 9.30am to 4pm, or at info@gmavsg.org. Specialist asbestos solicitors can advise which routes apply, and many work on a no win, no fee basis.

Sources: T&N Asbestos Trustee Company, GOV.UK, Employers' Liability Tracing Office, Greater Manchester Asbestos Victims Support Group. Photograph: Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Investigation works begin at former Turner Brothers asbestos factory in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Spodden Park Ltd has started investigations to locate buried asbestos at the derelict Turner Brothers factory, aiming for future redevelopment.
articles.content_html:
Spodden Park Ltd has commenced investigation works at the former Turner Brothers factory site in Spotland, Rochdale, to locate buried asbestos.

This site, once the world’s largest producer of asbestos, has been a concern for local residents due to the toxic materials associated with its history.

The investigations will be carried out by a specialist contractor over the coming weeks. Spodden Park Ltd assures that no asbestos will be disturbed during this phase, which aims to inform a safe remediation strategy for the site.

Heavy machinery will be used, but the company has stated that no buildings will be demolished during this process.

Locals have recently observed workers in overalls and diggers at the site, which has been nicknamed 'Rochdale's Chernobyl' due to its hazardous past.

The landowner has also issued warnings against trespassing, highlighting the dangers posed by the ongoing works and the need for enhanced security measures to prevent unauthorized access.

While the future plans for the site have not been fully disclosed, it is understood that Spodden Park Ltd intends to redevelop the area, potentially including housing and a park.

This follows a previous proposal for 650 homes in the early 2000s, which has since been scaled back.

articles.title: Six Rochdale Hornets players compete in international matches
articles.excerpt: This weekend, six players from Rochdale Hornets represented their countries in international rugby league fixtures, showcasing their skills on the international stage.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Hornets had a busy weekend as six players from their men's and women's teams participated in international rugby league matches. The fixtures included the Celtic Cup and a friendly match, highlighting the club's commitment to developing talent across all levels.

In Hawick, Scotland, Hornets captain Ross Whitmore played for the national team against Ireland, which featured new recruit Oli Whitford. Whitford, playing at full-back, scored the opening try in a match that ended with Ireland defeating Scotland 44-12.

Whitmore managed to score Scotland's only second-half try, demonstrating his determination on the field.

Meanwhile, four members of the Hornets women's squad represented the Netherlands in a match against Scotland, where they faced a challenging defeat of 54-0.

The Dutch Lionesses were captained for the first time by Hiske Blom, with Lisa Berding, Fiona Kalf, and Eva Peroti also contributing to the team's efforts.

The involvement of these players in international competitions reflects the depth of talent within Rochdale Hornets' programmes. The club expressed pride in their players' achievements and their ongoing commitment to rugby league.

Fans can look forward to more updates as the international tournaments progress.

articles.title: Rochdale Hornets assistant coach Ryan Jackson leaves for Keighley Cougars
articles.excerpt: Ryan Jackson has departed from Rochdale Hornets to join Keighley Cougars, having served as assistant coach since midway through the 2025 season.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Hornets have announced that assistant coach Ryan Jackson has left the club to take up a new position with Keighley Cougars. Jackson joined the Hornets midway through the 2025 season, initially in an unofficial capacity, supporting head coach Gary Thornton.

Prior to his time at Rochdale, Jackson spent four-and-a-half years as the assistant coach at Hunslet, where he played a significant role in the club's promotion to the Championship. He departed Hunslet in March 2025 before joining the Hornets.

The club expressed their gratitude to Jackson for his contributions and wished him well in his future endeavours. Jackson's departure marks a change in the coaching staff as the Hornets prepare for the upcoming season.

articles.title: Why are so many HMOs in Spotland? The debate over shared housing in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Spotland has one of the highest concentrations of Houses in Multiple Occupation in Rochdale borough. But why has the area become a hotspot for shared housing, and what does it mean for residents?
articles.content_html:
Walk through parts of Spotland and it quickly becomes apparent that the area has a far higher concentration of Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) than many other parts of Rochdale borough. Once occupied by single families, many larger Victorian and Edwardian terraced properties have gradually been converted into shared accommodation, making Spotland one of the borough's most significant clusters of HMOs.

The trend has become an increasingly important issue for residents, landlords and councillors alike. While HMOs provide an important source of affordable accommodation for many people, questions continue to be raised about whether too many are concentrated in particular neighbourhoods and what effect that has on local communities.

A House in Multiple Occupation is a property occupied by people from more than one household who share facilities such as kitchens or bathrooms. Larger HMOs with five or more occupants have long required mandatory licences, while since April 2025 Rochdale Council has expanded its additional licensing scheme to include many smaller HMOs with three or four occupants across the borough. The authority says the scheme is intended to improve housing standards, fire safety and property management.

Spotland's high concentration has developed over many years rather than overnight. Much of the housing stock consists of relatively large terraced homes close to Rochdale town centre, public transport, local shops and employment opportunities. Those characteristics make the area attractive for shared housing, particularly for single working adults, people on lower incomes and those needing flexible rented accommodation.

Supporters of HMOs argue they perform an essential role in the local housing market. They provide accommodation for key workers, young people leaving home, people whose relationships have broken down, those moving into the area for work and residents who simply cannot afford to rent an entire property on their own. With housing affordability remaining a challenge across Greater Manchester, shared accommodation is often one of the few realistic options available.

Critics, however, argue that excessive concentrations of HMOs can fundamentally change the character of established residential streets. Residents have raised concerns over increased parking pressures, higher population turnover, refuse management, antisocial behaviour linked to a minority of poorly managed properties and the gradual reduction in the number of traditional family homes available to buy.

Not every HMO creates problems. Many are professionally managed, well maintained and occupied by tenants who contribute positively to the local community. Councils and housing organisations frequently stress that poor management, rather than the concept of shared housing itself, is often at the heart of complaints.

Recognising those concerns, Rochdale Borough Council operates a licensing regime designed to ensure HMOs meet minimum standards covering fire precautions, room sizes, kitchen and bathroom facilities, property management and tenant safety. Licensed HMOs are recorded on a public register, allowing residents to check whether qualifying properties have been licensed.

The wider debate is about balance. Most housing experts accept that HMOs form an important part of the housing mix, but many also argue that large numbers concentrated within relatively small areas can place additional pressure on local services and alter neighbourhood dynamics. Achieving the right balance between providing affordable accommodation and maintaining stable, mixed communities remains one of the key challenges facing local authorities.

Spotland sits at the centre of that discussion in Rochdale. For some, its concentration of shared housing demonstrates the borough's ability to provide affordable homes for a diverse population. For others, it illustrates why councils should have stronger planning powers to prevent excessive clustering and preserve the long-term character of residential streets.

As demand for affordable rented accommodation continues to grow, the debate surrounding HMOs is unlikely to disappear. Future planning decisions, licensing enforcement and investment in housing quality will all play a part in determining whether areas such as Spotland can successfully balance the needs of tenants, landlords and long-established residents alike.
